Patient-reported symptoms:

  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
# Roimata's Vigil

Roimata Parata was fifty-three years old when the delivery truck hit him. He had been a financial analyst for twenty-eight years by then, a Samoan-New Zealand immigrant who had built a steady, predictable life in Portland—a career managing portfolios, a marriage of thirty years to his wife Aroha, a reputation at his firm for precision and calm judgment. The accident happened on a rain-slicked Tuesday in October as he crossed the parking lot of a grocery store, his arms full of bags. The truck's driver had misjudged the turn. Roimata heard the engine sound first—a heavy, accelerating growl—before he felt the impact that threw him across the asphalt. His ribs fractured. His left leg broke in two places. He lay there smelling the hot rubber of the tires, the acrid diesel fumes, his own blood mixing with rain and wet concrete. The driver's door opened with a metallic screech. Someone screamed. For what felt like hours but was probably minutes, Roimata remained conscious, waiting to know if he would die, listening to the chaos of voices and sirens that seemed to come from inside his own chest.

The physical recovery took fourteen months. The psychological one never really began, because Roimata never quite accepted that what happened to him was over. By the time he returned to work, he had already developed a habit of checking the fire exits in every room before he sat down—a quick visual scan that had become automatic, something he did without thinking, the way other men might adjust their glasses. At the office, he positioned his desk so that his back was never fully to the door. His colleagues assumed he was simply being cautious; they did not notice that his eyes were always moving, always cataloging the space around him, always aware of where the nearest exit lay.

The smells were worse than he had expected. Diesel fuel, which he encountered occasionally in parking lots or near delivery bays, would stop him mid-breath. His body would flood with adrenaline before his mind had even registered what he was smelling—his heart rate spiking, his palms going cold, his leg muscles tensing as though preparing to run or fight. The smell of hot rubber came later, triggered by worn tires or the friction of a car braking hard nearby. Aroha noticed that he had begun avoiding certain routes to the grocery store, certain parking lots altogether. When she asked him why, he could not quite articulate it. It was not rational. He knew, intellectually, that the probability of being hit again was vanishingly small. But his body did not believe what his mind knew. His body reacted first, always first, flooding him with certainty of danger before conscious thought could intervene.

The auditory triggers were perhaps the most insidious. Car sounds—the acceleration of an engine, the screech of tires, even the ordinary rumble of traffic—could transport him instantly back to that parking lot. The memory would arrive complete and overwhelming, not as something he was remembering but as something that was happening right now, in the present tense. He would hear the truck engine again, that terrible growl, and the memory would carry not just the visual image but the actual sounds, as though his ears were hearing them afresh. At night, he began waking in the dark, his body rigid with vigilance, needing to verify that he was safe, that Aroha was beside him, that the bedroom door was still locked.

Darkness had become a problem too. He could not enter a dark room without turning on every light. The parking garage at his office building made him nauseated. He had started arriving at work earlier and earlier, parking in the daylit areas near the entrance, accepting the longer walk rather than risk the shadowed levels below. Aroha had gently suggested therapy six months ago. He had refused. If he thought about the event, really thought about it, he was certain he would not be able to handle it—the memory would consume him entirely. It was safer to stay vigilant, to keep his guard up, to monitor the environment constantly. You never knew what could happen next. The world had shown him that much.

He is now sixty-three. Last month, he had a panic attack at his desk when a colleague's car backfired in the parking lot below. He left work at two in the afternoon and did not return for a week. Aroha finally insisted. She told him she was frightened of losing him, not to the truck, but to the life he had stopped living. This week, for the first time, Roimata made an appointment with a therapist. He is terrified of what it will mean to stop being vigilant, to stop believing that constant guard is the only thing keeping him alive.

missing_items: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
missing_explanations: The vignette includes the avoidance cognition ('If he thought about the event, really thought about it, he is certain he would not be able to handle it'), but this is presented as Roimata's own stated belief. However, the symptom item 'Thought Avoidance' specifically refers to a reported behavioral/cognitive pattern where the patient avoids thinking about the event due to fear of being overwhelmed. While the vignette contains the underlying thought, it does not clearly demonstrate that Roimata is actively avoiding thinking about the event as a coping strategy—only that he holds this belief. The distinction is subtle but clinically important: the symptom reflects active avoidance behavior motivated by this fear, not merely the presence of the fear itself.
